Topic 01 — Periodization & the General Adaptation Syndrome
Overload & the GAS
Why overload pays
The reward
  • High-volume/high-intensity phases (cycles/blocks) → big long-term gains.
Who it applies to
  • Athletes, tactical personnel (military, law enforcement, fire), general pop.
Why overload is risky
The risk
  • Stimulus > recovery capacity = overtraining (OT) → overtraining syndrome (OTS).
History
  • Recognized as early as 1866; also a problem in tactical populations.
Chapter goal
Chapter goal
  • Avoid unintended long-term ↓ performance — the opposite of the training goal.
Alarm Reaction
What happens
  • Stress hits → initial ↓ performance.
Resistance
What happens
  • Body resists the stressor → performance recovers.
Adaptation
What happens
  • Performance improves above baseline.
Too Much Stress
Selye's GAS
  • Stress too great → can't resist → persistent ↓ performance.
Outcome
  • Short-term = overreaching (OR); long-term = OT.
Paradigms
GAS & periodization
  • Models — real responses needn't look exactly like the classic diagram.
Academic questions
  • GAS validity in training.
  • Periodization models.
  • Fatigue accumulation from resistance exercise.
Consensus
Practitioner consensus
  • Most OT researchers + S&C pros recognize the complexity.
  • Understanding of OT/OR still far from complete.
Your Job
Your job
  • Create the proper overload AND adjust load so the athlete can recover and improve.
Resources
Limit
  • Time available, equipment & facilities.
Sport
Limit
  • Sport-specific training, governing-body regulations.
Schedule
Limit
  • Competition density, travel & time zones.
Athlete
Limit
  • Age, prior training history, injury/physical limits, menstrual cycle.
Life
Limit
  • Job, family demands & schedule, recreational activities.
Recovery Capacity
Key point
  • High-volume general-prep phases are effective — until volume/intensity exceeds the recovery capacity of the individual or team.

Overtraining &

Topic 02 — Overtraining & Overreaching Defined
OT, OR & Definitions
Overtraining (OT)
The process
  • Excessive volumes/intensities of training.
Overtraining syndrome (OTS)
The result
  • Collection of symptoms + long-term performance impairment (weeks → months or longer).
Impairment Required
Key point
  • To be overtrained = have OTS and the required long-term impairment.
  • Performance impairment is necessary — but not all impairments are alike.
Overtraining (OT)
Definition
  • Accumulated training and/or non-training stress → long-term ↓ performance capacity ± physiological/psychological maladaptation signs.
Recovery
  • Weeks–months.
Overreaching (OR)
Definition
  • Same definition — but short-term ↓ performance.
Recovery
  • Days–several weeks.
  • Lower severity, faster recovery.
Source
Position stand
  • ECSS–ACSM joint task force position stand (updated 2013).
"Syndrome"
Meaning
  • Symptoms associated with each other — some may be non-training.
Overload
Terms used
  • Overworked, overstressed, overfatigued, burnout, excessive fatigue.
Performance
Terms used
  • Underperformance, unexplained underperformance, staleness, stagnation.
Recovery
Terms used
  • Underrecovered, imbalance of work & recovery, chronic fatigue.
Adaptation
Terms used
  • Failure to adapt, maladaptation, stressful training syndrome.
One Problem
Why it matters
  • Terminology chaos → position stands + consensus statements.
Constant
  • Symptoms vary by individual and training type — but performance is always impaired.
Topic 02 — Overtraining & Overreaching Defined
Three Levels of Impairment
Common Ground
All three
  • All three = ↓ performance.
They differ in
  • Recovery time, supercompensation, and symptom burden.
FOR
Functional overreaching
  • Short recovery → supercompensation.
NFOR
Nonfunctional overreaching
  • Longer recovery → back to baseline only.
OTS
Overtraining syndrome
  • Long-term impairment → weeks to months.
What It Is
Definition
  • Planned micro/mesocycle of ↑ volume or intensity.
  • Short-term ↓ performance; recovery in days–weeks.
How It Works
Mechanism
  • Examples: preseason camps with 2–3 sessions/day; general-prep blocks.
  • Recover → supercompensation.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • Beneficial if appropriate recovery is allowed. Commonly used by successful coaches.
  • e.g. Periodization block that dips performance, then peaks it.
What It Is
Definition
  • Like FOR, but greater short-term accumulated fatigue and longer recovery.
How It Works
Mechanism
  • No supercompensation — only returns to baseline.
  • Serves no useful function.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • Athlete was stressed for no benefit. Fix the load.
What It Is
Definition
  • Chronic stressful training → ↓ performance.
  • Recovery: weeks → months or longer.
How It Works
Mechanism
  • Affects more than performance — physiological + psychological signs.
  • Can include non-training stressors.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • Serious: greatly interferes with or halts competition training.
  • e.g. Distance runners: recovery up to a year (Lehmann).
What It Is
Definition
  • Mildest form of impairment.
  • Sometimes called a type of OT.
What To Do
Challenge
  • Hard to separate from normal plateaus — all seriously trained athletes get them.
Fix
  • If caused by an inappropriate load → adjust the program.
Topic 02 — Overtraining & Overreaching Defined
Two Faces of OTS
Origin
Named by Israel (1976)
  • By how the autonomic nervous system responds to training stress.
SOTS
Sympathetic OTS
  • ↑ epinephrine response to training.
POTS
Parasympathetic OTS
  • Parasympathetic predominance; ↓ sympathetic response.
What It Is
Definition
  • Primary feature: ↑ epinephrine response to exercise and training.
  • Hypothetical until shown in resistance-exercise overtrained subjects (Fry 1994).
How It Works
Mechanism
  • Chronic ↑ catecholamines → down-regulation of β2 receptors in skeletal muscle.
  • → impaired muscle contractility.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • Hypothesized to precede POTS. Rated "strong" for strength & power training.
What It Is
Definition
  • Parasympathetic predominance; a.k.a. Addisonoid syndrome (often ↓ cortisol).
  • Mostly aerobic endurance athletes with huge volumes.
How It Works
Mechanism
  • Primary symptom (besides ↓ performance): diminished sympathetic (epinephrine) response — "adrenal exhaustion."
  • Classic: Lehmann's middle-distance runners.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • ↓ resting HR looks like fitness in trained athletes → tricky to diagnose.
  • POTS doesn't cause the impairment — it's a symptom cluster. Recovery up to a year.
Topic 02 — Overtraining & Overreaching Defined

Look-Alike Conditions

Psychological
OT/OTS share features with clinical depression, PTSD, other psychological conditions.
RED-S
Relative energy deficiency syndrome (formerly female athlete triad) — symptoms overlap OTS.
Each can contribute to the other.
Root causes differ. S&C role: recognize when to refer — RED-S needs trained professionals.
Topic 03

The Continuum
& Contributing
Factors

Topic 03 — Overtraining Continuum & Contributing Factors
Continuum & Balance
Core Idea
Same process, different sports
  • Proper training adaptations differ by sport — so do OT contributing factors, impairments, and physiological responses.
Endurance
Endurance sport
  • Distance runner.
  • Aerobic-driven OT.
Hybrid
Hybrid sport
  • Wrestler.
  • Aerobic + anaerobic.
Anaerobic
Anaerobic sport
  • Shot-putter.
  • Strength/power.
Resistance
Resistance exercise
  • High-intensity, high-volume, or both → separate OT pathways.
Acute Fatigue
Stage 1
  • Typical training response.
FOR
Stage 2
  • Effective training.
NFOR
Stage 3
  • Ineffective training.
OTS: SOTS
Stage 4
  • Anaerobic; strength & power.
OTS: POTS
Stage 5
  • Endurance; volume-dominant.
Key Point
Severity
  • Levels may overlap, but each step is more serious and needs longer, more intense recovery.
  • OT is complex and multidisciplinary.
Balanced
Balanced training
  • Stress countered by adequate recovery → long-term progression.
Overtraining
Overtraining
  • Excessive training, inadequate recovery, or both.
Undertraining
Undertraining
  • Inadequate load → suboptimal performance.
The Challenge
Challenge
  • Find the balance that maximizes long-term adaptation.
Topic 03 — Overtraining Continuum & Contributing Factors
Contributing Factors
Volume
Volume
  • Total reps, volume-load, mechanical work, metabolic work, training frequency.
Intensity
Intensity
  • Relative (%RM), absolute (kg), perceived effort.
Either or Both
Excess
  • Excess of either — or both combined — creates an OT stimulus.
Biggest share
  • Sport practice + competition are the biggest part of total stress.
Periodization
Error
  • Incorrectly designed long-term plan → OT even in a "periodized" program.
Variation
Error
  • Lack of load variation → quantified by %CV = SD ÷ mean.
Taper
Error
  • No appropriate taper (tapers enhance performance testing).
Sport Load
Error
  • Sport-specific practice + competition stress ignored.
Monitoring
Error
  • Not tracking training characteristics — maybe the most important way to prescribe load.
Allostatic Load
Definition
  • Antecedents (contributing factors) → stress responses = allostatic load ("wear and tear"; concept from 1993).
Training + Recovery
Primary factors
  • Training + recovery process itself.
Outside Training
Secondary factors
  • Outside training & competition — still contribute to OTS.
Two-way link
  • Secondary factors can cause OTS and be caused by it.
Required link
  • These are contributing, not direct, causes. Performance impairment is the required link to OTS.
Medical
Factors
  • Illness, disease, misdiagnosis, injury.
Sleep
Factors
  • Sleep quality, circadian rhythms.
Nutrition
Factors
  • Nutritional quality.
Travel
Factors
  • Travel schedule, time zones, competition density.
Mental
Factors
  • Mental well-being, motivational orientation.
Life
Factors
  • Family & peers, job/employment, multi-sport.
Topic 04

Under-
performance

Topic 04 — Underperformance
Not All Is Overtraining
Overtraining
One cause
  • One cause of underperformance.
  • Requires impairment — and long-term recovery.
Everything Else
Other causes
  • Many other factors ↓ performance — some outside your control.
  • Recognize them → choose the right response.
Key Point
Key point
  • Seldom are all training + competition components in synchrony. Not all underperformance is OT/OR.
Training
Cause
  • Undertraining; poorly structured periodization; training monotony.
Peaking
Cause
  • Peak not timed to the competition schedule.
Practice
Cause
  • Inadequate sport practice; poor contest strategy.
Climate
Cause
  • Motivational climate.
Non-training
Cause
  • Competition density, mental state, multi-sport, family & peers.
Link
Key point
  • Same stressors that feed allostatic load can also drive underperformance — with no OT present.
What It Looks Like
Appearance
  • Performance impaired at the key event.
  • Overtraining gets the blame.
What It Is
Actual cause
  • Well-designed program, but the training peak ≠ competition date.
  • Cause = inappropriate timing, not excess training.
Check First
Rule
  • Check the periodization calendar before diagnosing OT.
Topic 05

Performance
Variables
Affected

Topic 05 — Performance-Related Variables Affected
Variables Affected
What Drops
OT can impair
  • ↓ strength, power, or speed
  • ↓ rate of force development
  • ↓ anaerobic endurance
  • ↓ aerobic endurance
  • ↓ cognitive function
Order & Caution
Order
  • Any one or more, in any order.
Caution
  • Hard to create OTS in the lab; field data lack control → interpret carefully.
Speed
Sprinting
  • Most sensitive — drops first.
Power
Force × velocity
  • Drops next.
Max Strength
1RM
  • One of the last to drop.
Takeaway
"Strength is well-protected"
  • Monitoring only 1RM misses early OT.
First affected
  • High-velocity activities.
Within Days
Markers
  • Perceptions of recovery (very high sensitivity).
  • EMG-to-force efficiency.
Up to 1 Week
Markers
  • Self-efficacy, desire to train; isokinetic + stimulated force.
  • Vertical jump kinetics + kinematics.
1+ Weeks
Markers
  • Sprinting.
  • Resistance-exercise power + velocity.
Warning System
Key point
  • Psychological variables + speed/power = your earliest warning system.
Last
Marker
  • 1RM / multijoint strength (low sensitivity).
Seldom
Marker
  • Vertical jump height.
Slower
Marker
  • Training capacity (tolerance of high volumes + frequent sessions).
Unknown
Marker
  • Eccentric strength; multijoint RFD.
Monitoring
Key point
  • Include speed, power, and psych measures — not strength alone — in your athlete monitoring program.
Topic 06

Physiological
Mechanisms

Topic 06 — Physiological Mechanisms
Physiological Mechanisms
Result
Result
  • Mechanisms can be caused by an OT stimulus.
Scope
  • Not all OT is identical → symptoms vary by individual + program.
  • OTS can affect many systems (nervous, endocrine, immune, muscular, orthopedic).
Contributor
Contributor
  • Pre-existing issues add to allostatic load → can contribute to OTS.
Four Strong
Best-supported mechanisms
  • Autonomic nervous system — SOTS / POTS disruption
  • Endocrine — T, cortisol, T:C, GH, receptors
  • Glycogen deficiency — fuel availability
  • Muscle cell signaling — cellular adaptation pathways
Strong
Mechanisms
  • Glycogen deficiency
  • ANS disruption
  • SOTS (strength/power)
  • POTS (aerobic)
  • Endocrine disruption (T, cortisol, T/C, GH, receptors)
  • Muscle cellular signaling
Likely
Mechanisms
  • Circadian rhythm disruption
  • Cytokine disruption
  • ↓ immune function
  • Dietary insufficiencies
  • Motor unit recruitment
  • Orthopedic inhibition
  • Impaired cognitive function
Possible
Mechanisms
  • Glutamine deficiency
  • Tissue trauma
  • Central fatigue theory
  • Oxidative stress
  • Neural modifications
Inconclusive
Mechanisms
  • Sex-related factors
How To Read
Key point
  • Rating = strength of supporting data — not whether the mechanism matters.
What It Is
Definition
  • ANS responds rapidly to OT.
  • Israel (1976): split into sympathetic vs parasympathetic patterns.
How It Works
Mechanism
  • SOTS: ↑ epinephrine → β2 down-regulation (strength/power).
  • POTS: ↓ sympathetic response (aerobic training).
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • Mode of training predicts the pattern — monitor accordingly.
  • Resting HR alone can mislead in POTS.
What It Is
Definition
  • Changes in testosterone, cortisol, T:C ratio, GH, hormone receptors.
How It Works
Mechanism
  • Studied in OT research (Adlercreutz; Fry & Kraemer; Nicoll).
  • Rated strong.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • "Hormonal variables indicate stress, not OT."
  • Don't diagnose OT from a hormone panel.
What It Is
Definition
  • Depleted glycogen stores — rated strong (la Torre 2023).
How It Works
Mechanism
  • Linked with dietary insufficiencies (fats, protein, carbohydrate, micronutrients) — rated likely.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • Appropriate diet: adequate kcal, protein, glycogen repletion, vitamins/minerals, fluids.
What It Is
Definition
  • Altered signaling pathways in skeletal muscle — rated strong (Nicoll 2016, 2019).
How It Works
Mechanism
  • Measured via heat shock proteins, cell-signaling pathways, receptors.
  • Muscle fiber maladaptation can follow.
Training Implication
Takeaway
  • Research-level markers — not routine S&C tests.
  • Practical focus = prevent via load + recovery.
Topic 07

Assessment

Topic 07 — Assessment of Overreaching & Overtraining
Assessing OR & OT
Match the Test
Principle
  • Tests must be matched to the training and physiological system involved.
Four Qualities
A good monitoring program is
  • Valid — specific to the training or system
  • Reliable — consistent results
  • Sensitive — detects the training/competition stimulus
  • Easy to use — fits into routine monitoring; fast turnaround
Category I
Frequency
  • Daily.
Features
  • Easy, inexpensive, rapid results.
  • Convenient for coach + athlete.
Category II
Frequency
  • Every few days.
Features
  • More complex, longer questionnaires.
  • Rapid turnaround.
Category III
Frequency
  • Occasional (e.g. monthly).
Features
  • Involved, intrusive, expensive.
  • Slow turnaround.
Tiered Approach
Bernacikova
  • Start with Category I; only if it flags a problem → II → III.
  • Avoids unnecessary testing.
Purpose
Why test performance
  • Impaired performance is required for OT — performance tests = early detection.
Load
Tests
  • Monitored internal + external training loads; RPE/lactate.
Cardio
Tests
  • Resting HR, recovery HR, HRV, muscle O₂ saturation.
Capacity
Tests
  • Anaerobic thresholds, VO₂max, ability to repeat a GXT, ability to finish a session.
Jump
Tests
  • Height, kinetics, kinematics, stiffness, eccentric utilization ratio.
Resistance
Tests
  • Max strength, velocity-load + power-load profiles, bar velocity at same absolute load, isometric mid-thigh pull.
Endurance
Tests
  • Muscle endurance tests, rate of force production.
Sprint
Tests
  • Acceleration, first-step speed, deceleration, max velocity.
Agility
Tests
  • Change of direction, reaction + movement time.
Other
Tests
  • Cognitive processing tests; diet + sleep records; coaches' assessment.
Blood
Tests
  • Hormones, neurohormones, interleukins/cytokines, muscle-damage markers, immune factors.
Cardiovascular
Tests
  • Resting HR, HRV, oxygen uptake, muscle O₂ saturation.
Muscle
Tests
  • Heat shock proteins, cell-signaling pathways, receptors.
Neuromuscular
Tests
  • Motor unit recruitment, EMG activity.
Orthopedic
Tests
  • Joint inflammation, inhibitory input.
Caution
Reality
  • S&C pros don't usually order these.
Key point
  • Meaningfulness is equivocal — no reliable OTS biomarker yet.
Effort
Tools
  • RPE (Borg), CR10 RPE.
Mood
Tools
  • POMS (37-item version available).
Stress
Tools
  • DALDA, RESTQ-Sport, ARSS/SRSS, TQR, Hooper Index.
OT-specific
Tools
  • Resistance Exercise Overtraining Questionnaire (Fry).
Sleep
Tools
  • PSQI, Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire.
Why Use Them
Key point
  • Subjective measures may be more useful than quantitative ones for monitoring OT risk.
Length
Ask
  • How long? How many items?
Validated
Ask
  • Has it been validated?
Wording
Ask
  • Easy for the athlete to understand?
Processing
Ask
  • Rapid data turnaround?
No Coercion
Ask
  • Can it be answered freely?
Sensitive
Ask
  • Responds to an OT stimulus?
Motivational Climate
Effect
  • Coach-created climate → big effect on athlete effort, enjoyment, retention.
Tools
  • TEOSQ, PMCSQ, Caring Climate Scale (less frequent).
Mental Health
Helps
  • Mindfulness, caring + task-oriented climate, mood awareness help.
  • Coach mental health also affects athletes.
Takeaway
Key point
  • Mentally healthy athletes may withstand stressful training better.

Recovery
Methods &
Strategies

Topic 08 — Recovery Methods & Strategies
Recovery Strategies
Modify the Program
Rated strong
  • ↓ volume, frequency, intensity — or stop training.
When
  • Mandatory when OT has occurred.
Taper
Rated strong
  • Related to modifying the program.
Reality Check
Slow onset
  • OT onset is complex + slow; it is not rapidly reversed.
Practicality
  • Full cessation isn't always practical.
Overreaching
Recovery
  • Training cessation → baseline in as little as 1 week.
OT: Resistance
Recovery
  • Up to 4 weeks after high-intensity resistance exercise.
OT: Endurance
Recovery
  • Months to a year after high-volume distance running.
Common Factor
Key point
  • In each case volume/intensity was immediately cut or removed.
Strong
Modality
  • Quality sleep
Promising
Modalities
  • Cold-water immersion
  • Mindfulness-based interventions
  • Carbohydrates
Possible
Modalities
  • Hydration, compression garments
  • Vibration foam rolling, myofascial release
  • Acupuncture, red-light therapy
Inconclusive / Poor
Inconclusive
  • Massage; other cryotherapy
Poor
  • Bed rest — good for injuries, poor for fitness
Caveat
Key point
  • Few data support these for OT specifically — but therapists use them successfully for medical conditions.
Diet Base
Diet comes first
  • Adequate kcal, protein, glycogen repletion, vitamins/minerals, fluids.
Promising
Supplement
  • Carbohydrates
Possible
Supplements
  • Protein, branched-chain amino acids
  • Nitrates, L-glutamine, vitamins
  • Oral ATP
Diet First
Key point
  • Dietary supplements "may help" (recovery drinks, protein/carb, creatine, oral ATP) — diet comes first.
Topic 08 — Recovery Methods & Strategies
Risk & Prevention
Key Considerations
Remember
  • Not all types of OT are identical.
  • Strength is well-protected; speed + power more sensitive.
  • Psychological variables may be effective markers.
  • Hormonal variables indicate stress, not OT.
  • Orthopedic problems present different OTS.
  • Autonomic activity responds rapidly; muscle fiber maladaptation can follow.
Monitoring
Risk
  • Lack of close monitoring (rest days, prior exposure to stressful training).
Objective
Risk
  • Lack of any objective monitoring.
Outside
Risk
  • Training + activities outside the weight room.
Remote
Risk
  • Virtual coaching with no face-to-face contact.
Athlete
Risk
  • Higher-level, more fit athletes.
Recovery
Risk
  • Unmonitored recovery training sessions.
Peak Blocks
Risk
  • Olympic/world championship training blocks.
Taper
Risk
  • Failure to implement an appropriate taper.
Coach
Risk
  • Coaching by someone with little experience or training.
Environment
Risk
  • Change of training environment (heat, cold, humidity, altitude).
Controllable
Key point
  • Most of these are controllable.
Recovery
Strategy
  • Use active + passive recovery; allow ≥1 routine rest day — rest days are critical.
Sessions
Strategy
  • Limit excessively long sessions + too many sessions per day.
Volume
Strategy
  • Caution with large volume increases (>30%).
Exposure
Strategy
  • Prior exposure to stressful training ↑ tolerance.
Variation
Strategy
  • Vary the stimulus; use periodized training; avoid excessive training to failure.
Coordinate
Strategy
  • Coordinate resistance exercise with sport training + other conditioning.
Recover
Strategy
  • Sleep, diet, mental skills.
Diet
Strategy
  • Adequate kcal, protein, glycogen repletion, vitamins/minerals, fluids.
Supplements
Strategy
  • Recovery drinks, protein + carb, creatine, oral ATP may help.
Monitor
Strategy
  • Outside stressors + internal/external loads — run an athlete monitoring program.
